[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic diagnostic dilemma in breast pathology: distinguishing between fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor — both fibroepithelial lesions sharing overlapping clinical and imaging features but with critical differences in biological behavior and management. The patient is an adult female (age not specified, but fibroadenomas peak in 20s–30s; phyllodes tumors more common in 40s–50s), presenting with a stable, painless, well-circumscribed, solid breast mass — highly suggestive of benign etiology. Imaging (ultrasound) shows non-suspicious features, and core biopsy reveals a fibroepithelial lesion with rounded contour and overgrowth of fibrous and glandular tissue — the hallmark of fibroadenoma *morphologically*. However, the biopsy is insufficient to rule out phyllodes tumor because definitive diagnosis hinges on histologic assessment of stromal features not yet reported: stromal cellularity, mitotic count, cytologic atypia, and architectural leaf-like fronding — all required per WHO criteria. While phyllodes remains a *possibility*, its prevalence is far lower than fibroadenoma (~0.3–1% of breast biopsies vs. ~10–15%), and the absence of red-flag clinical/imaging/pathologic features strongly favors the more common, benign entity. Final diagnosis must await full histopathologic evaluation — but *pre-test probability*, combined with stable clinical course, benign imaging, and classic core morphology, points decisively to fibroadenoma as the single most likely diagnosis.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Fibroadenoma
